indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.2.1: Demonstrate knowledge of generation of electricity, its transmission and transformation into other forms of energy
indicator.objective: Recognise the importance of safety when using electricity

skills.description: Identify safe practices when using electricity
Explain simply why an action is unsafe
Recognise why electrical gadgets are covered with plastic or rubber

misconceptions: You can touch a socket if your hands are only a little wet.
Plastic covers are just for decoration.
Only naked wires are dangerous; covered wires are always safe.
Electricity is safe to play with if it is from a battery.
Wood and rubber are dangerous because they burn.

questions.stem: Which of these is a safe way to use electricity?
options: Touching a socket with wet hands
Keeping your hands dry before touching a switch
Pulling a plug by its wire
hints: Water and electricity are dangerous together.
Dry hands are safer.
questions.explanation: You should always keep your hands dry before touching electrical switches or sockets.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wet hands are fine if the water is clean.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT safe?
options: Using a dry cloth to hold a plug
Sticking your fingers into a socket
Turning off the light before changing a bulb
Using a wooden stick to push a switch
hints: Never put your fingers where electricity flows.
You could get a shock.
questions.explanation: Sticking your fingers into a socket is very dangerous and can cause a severe electric shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize how dangerous sockets are.

questions.stem: Why are electrical wires covered with plastic or rubber?
options: To protect people from getting a shock
hints: Plastic does not let electricity pass through.
It keeps you safe.
questions.explanation: Plastic and rubber are insulators. They stop electricity from flowing into your body and giving you a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the covering is just for decoration or to keep the wire clean.

questions.stem: Kwame sees a wire with the plastic covering peeled off. What should he do?
options: Touch it to see if it works
hints: Naked wires are dangerous.
Do not touch it.
questions.explanation: A wire with the covering peeled off (naked wire) is dangerous. Kwame should not touch it and should tell an adult.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is safe to touch wires if they want to check them.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to touch a switch with wet hands?
options: Water can conduct electricity and cause a shock
hints: Water and electricity do not mix.
You could get an electric shock.
questions.explanation: Water can conduct (carry) electricity. Touching a switch with wet hands can cause an electric shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water protects you from electricity.

questions.stem: Ama wants to unplug the television. What is the safest way to do it?
options: Pull the plug itself with dry hands
hints: Hold the plastic part of the plug.
Make sure hands are dry.
questions.explanation: You should always hold the plug itself with dry hands, not pull the wire, to avoid damaging the wire or getting a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils often pull the wire because it is faster.

questions.stem: Which of these is a dangerous thing to do near a live electric wire?
hints: The kite string can touch the wire.
You could get a shock.
questions.explanation: Flying a kite near electric wires is dangerous because the string can touch the wires and cause a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize string can conduct electricity.

questions.stem: Why is it safer to use a wooden stick to push a fallen electric wire away from you than to use your hand?
options: Wood is heavier than your hand
Wood is an insulator and does not carry electricity well
Wood is colder than your hand
hints: Wood does not let electricity pass through easily.
It protects you.
questions.explanation: Wood is an insulator (or a poor conductor), so it helps protect you from getting a shock when moving a live wire.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any solid object protects them.

questions.stem: If you see someone getting an electric shock, why should you NOT touch them with your bare hands?
options: They will be too heavy to pull
The electricity can pass into your body too
hints: Electricity travels through conductors.
You could get shocked as well.
questions.explanation: Touching someone who is being shocked can allow the electricity to flow into your body as well. You should turn off the power source first.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can just pull the person away.

questions.stem: Why is it important to wear shoes (especially with rubber soles) when dealing with electricity?
options: Because shoes make you run faster
Because rubber is an insulator and protects you from shocks
Because shoes make you look good
Because shoes keep your feet warm
hints: Rubber is an insulator.
It stops electricity from going into your feet.
questions.explanation: Rubber-soled shoes act as insulators, helping to protect you from electric shocks by stopping electricity from reaching the ground through your body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know rubber is an insulator.

questions.stem: Ama is playing with a broken electric socket. Is it safe?
options: Yes, if you use a stick
Yes, it is just a game
hints: Broken sockets can have naked wires.
Do not touch them.
questions.explanation: Playing with a broken socket is very dangerous. It might still have power and could cause a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a broken item is safe to play with.

questions.stem: Which of these materials would be best to make the handle of an electric iron?
hints: You need an insulator.
Copper and iron are metals.
questions.explanation: Rubber is an insulator, so it is safe to use for the handle of an iron to prevent the user from getting a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think metals are good for handles.

questions.stem: Kofi sees an electric fire starting in his house. What should he do FIRST?
options: Tell an adult and try to turn off the main power switch safely
Touch the fire with his hands
hints: Water and electricity are dangerous together.
Get help and stop the power.
questions.explanation: You should never throw water on an electrical fire. The best step is to tell an adult and safely cut off the electricity supply.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water can put out any fire.

questions.stem: Why is overloading a socket (plugging too many appliances into one socket) dangerous?
options: It can cause the wires to overheat and start a fire
It makes the appliances run faster
hints: Too much electricity through one wire.
It can get very hot.
questions.explanation: Plugging too many appliances into one socket pulls too much electricity, which can overheat the wires and cause a fire.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the limits of a socket.

questions.stem: Which of these is an unsafe electrical practice?
options: Using a dry cloth to clean a switch
Using a fork to get bread out of a plugged-in toaster
Turning off the lights before leaving the room
hints: Metal conducts electricity.
The toaster is still plugged in.
questions.explanation: Using a metal object like a fork in a plugged-in appliance is very dangerous because you could easily touch live parts and get shocked.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize everyday actions can be dangerous.

questions.stem: Why are power lines outside usually covered with thick plastic or rubber, and sometimes hung high up?
options: To protect birds and people from getting shocked
hints: They carry high power.
They are out in the open.
questions.explanation: Covering them with insulators and hanging them high helps protect people and animals from accidental contact and shocks.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think about safety in outdoor power lines.

questions.stem: Why is it important to have a qualified electrician do wiring in a house?
options: Because they are the only ones who can buy wires
Because they know how to do it safely and avoid dangerous mistakes
hints: Wiring is dangerous work.
A mistake can cause a fire.
questions.explanation: Electricians are trained to install wiring safely. Poor wiring can lead to electric shocks or fires.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anyone can fix wires.

questions.stem: Look at pictures of these scenarios: (1) touching a socket with wet hands, (2) pulling a plug by the wire, (3) turning off a switch with dry hands. Show your teacher which one is safe and explain why.

criteria.description: Identifies turning off the switch with dry hands as the safe option
Explains that water and pulling wires are dangerous

hints: Which action keeps hands dry?
Which actions are unsafe?
questions.explanation: This tests identifying safe and unsafe electricity practices.

questions.stem: Explain why it is dangerous to use a metal spoon to unplug a faulty electric kettle.

criteria.description: States that it can cause an electric shock

hints: What is the spoon made of?
What does metal do with electricity?
questions.explanation: Metal is a good conductor of electricity. Using a metal spoon can cause the electricity to flow into your body, giving you a severe shock.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher three rules for staying safe with electricity.

criteria.description: States one valid safety rule (e.g., dry hands)
States a second valid rule (e.g., don't pull wires)
States a third valid rule (e.g., don't climb poles)

hints: What should your hands be like?
Should you put things in sockets?
questions.explanation: Rules include: keep hands dry, never stick objects into sockets, don't pull plugs by the wire, and tell an adult about broken wires.
